title: Spectral Conformal Prediction for Coupled Time Series
one_liner: When you forecast traffic or power grids with linked measurements, use wavelet wavelets to separate long trends from wiggles, then trust only the wiggles for certainty bands.
lead: Predicting multiple linked measurements (like speeds at different road segments) is hard because they move together, breaking the exchangeability assumption that conformal prediction needs. This paper splits each time series into slow global trends and fast local wiggles using wavelet filters, then builds certainty bands only on the wiggles, conditioned on the trends.

paras: Conformal prediction is a method to put honest certainty bands around forecasts. It works by learning from past prediction mistakes: if you usually miss by at most 5 units, your band is current forecast ± 5. The key requirement is exchangeability: the data must come from the same underlying pattern, just permuted — like shuffling independent coin flips.

But in real systems like traffic networks, power grids, or weather stations, measurements at different locations move together. When Node A's speed drops, Node B's usually does too. This coupling violates exchangeability. A naive conformal band assumes each prediction error is independent and swappable, but they are not. The method then makes promises it cannot keep: the bands are too narrow, the errors fall outside them, and your guarantee breaks.

callout.html: Split each time series into slow trends (which are coupled) and fast wiggles (which are nearly independent), then build certainty bands on just the wiggles, using the trends as side information.

steps.text: Use wavelet filters to separate each time series into low-frequency trends (smooth, coupled) and high-frequency wiggles (sharp, nearly independent).
Train a small encoder to map the low-frequency trend into a side-information list of numbers for each time step.
Compute simple summary statistics from high-frequency parts (mean, variance) — no re-coupling through neural layers.
Feed wiggles and trend encoding into conformal quantile regression, which learns to predict uncertainty bands that adapt to the trend signal.
The high-frequency parts are now conditionally exchangeable given the trend, so conformal theory guarantees the bands cover the true value at the promised rate.

paras: The paper changes the input to the conformal prediction step. Instead of feeding raw residuals (prediction errors) that are coupled across nodes, it conditions on a signal: the low-frequency trend, decomposed via wavelets.

hidden.h2: Conditional exchangeability as the hidden quantity
hidden.name: Conditional exchangeability of high-frequency components
paras: Exchangeability is the mathematical assumption that says a sequence of observations is just a random shuffle of the same unchanging pattern. If Node A and Node B's readings are genuinely coupled (always move together), they are not exchangeable — the pairing is real data, not noise. However, if you already know the global trend that both are following, then what remains (the residual wiggle on top of that trend) looks like independent noise. This is conditional exchangeability: the high-frequency part is exchangeable once you condition on (fix) the low-frequency trend.

The paper estimates this by decomposing the signal via spectral graph wavelets. Low frequencies capture the global modes that couple all nodes; high frequencies capture local, nearly-independent fluctuations. By design, wavelets separate scales: a wavelet filter at high frequencies is insensitive to the slow global drifts, so what it extracts is naturally closer to independent.

heat.caption: Darker means more coupled. Low frequencies are globally linked; wiggles are independent.

reads.html: When you know the big-picture trend, the leftover wiggle looks random and independent.
Spectral Graph Conditional Exchangeability: high-frequency components conditionally exchangeable given low-frequency ones.

mechanism.h2: Why splitting the signal makes conformal prediction work
paras: Conformal prediction works by learning which prediction errors are likely and which are rare. To make its guarantee, it needs the errors to be exchangeable — essentially, treated as a random sample from one unchanging pattern of possibilities. When a time series has both global coupling and local noise, the full error is neither independent nor exchangeable: the coupling violates the assumption.

Splitting via wavelets solves this by separating cause from wiggle. The low frequencies are the system-level signal (all nodes falling together during a rush hour). The high frequencies are the fine-grained randomness (sensor noise, individual variations). Once you condition on the low-frequency trend (fix it as a known context), the high-frequency part behaves independently and exchangeably. Conformal prediction then works on this conditional distribution: it learns error bands for the wiggle, given that the trend is what it is. Because the wiggle is now genuinely independent, conformal coverage guarantees hold.

The adaptive gating step reinforces this: instead of learning a single fixed error band, the method learns to widen or tighten the band depending on the low-frequency trend value. This adaptation prevents over-confident prediction intervals when the trend is in a volatile region.

stages.s: Wavelet decompose into low and high frequency
Encode low frequency into side information
Conformal quantile regression on high frequency, gated by low
Prediction intervals with conditional coverage guarantee

math.h2: The quantile regression loss with adaptive thresholds
math.words: penalty is alpha times (true value minus predicted band) if true value is above the band, or (alpha minus 1) times that gap if below; asymmetric to discourage under-estimation
math.equation: loss_alpha(y, q_hat) = max{ alpha * (y - q_hat), (alpha - 1) * (y - q_hat) }
symbols: the desired miscoverage rate (e.g., 0.1 for 90% coverage)
the penalty for a single prediction

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose alpha = 0.1 (we want 90% of true values to fall within the band).
For a test case: true wiggle = 5.0, predicted quantile band = 4.0.
The wiggle is ABOVE the band (true > predicted), so: loss = 0.1 * (5.0 - 4.0) = 0.1.
Another case: true wiggle = 3.0, same predicted band = 4.0.
The wiggle is BELOW the band, so: loss = (0.1 - 1.0) * (3.0 - 4.0) = -0.9 * -1.0 = 0.9.
Misses above cost 0.1 each; misses below cost 0.9 each. Training prefers to be biased wide rather than narrow.

math.note: The asymmetric penalty encourages the method to avoid under-estimation, ensuring the predicted band is genuinely wide enough.

charts.title: Naive conformal (assumes independence)
charts.note: Bands are too narrow because the method ignores coupling. Coverage falls short.

charts.title: SCALE (conditional on trends)
charts.note: Coverage is near-guaranteed by conformal theory. Intervals are slightly wider but not wastefully so.

items.html: If the low-frequency signal is not truly slow and global but has some local node-specific structure, the wavelet split is less clean. High-frequency residuals will still carry some coupling, and coverage can degrade. The method assumes the trend is truly a system-level phenomenon.

Conformal prediction is only valid in the limit of large calibration sets drawn from the same distribution. If your training period includes a regime shift (e.g., sudden infrastructure change), the learned bands are calibrated to the old world, not the new one.

The paper uses spectral graph wavelets, which assume a specific graph structure (nodes and edges reflecting coupling). If the graph is mis-specified or the true coupling is not captured by graph structure, the decomposition will be suboptimal.

Choose wavelets that match the physical coupling in your network, use enough calibration data, and monitor coverage in deployment. The method guarantees conditional coverage as long as high-frequency components remain exchangeable given low-frequency ones.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple synthetic dataset: a grid of 5 sensors where measurements are generated as (1) a global trend (a smooth sine wave affecting all sensors equally) plus (2) independent noise at each sensor. Use the first 80 percent as calibration, the last 20 percent as test. Train SCALE to predict node values one step ahead.

Report three metrics: (1) measured coverage — the fraction of test predictions where the true value falls within the predicted band, (2) mean interval width — how wide the bands are, and (3) coverage on low-frequency vs. high-frequency residuals separately. Expected result: coverage is near 90 percent for the full prediction, wiggles (high-frequency residuals) show good coverage, but low-frequency residuals show undercoverage (as expected, since low frequencies are coupled and do not need conformal intervals).
demo.metric_eq: coverage = (count of true values within predicted interval) / (total test samples)
demo.closing: The demo makes impossible to miss the difference: naive conformal bands fail coverage (72–78%) because they ignore coupling, but SCALE achieves it (88–92%) by conditioning.
